Concepts in this composition

Legitimately many (Lee Sharks, #1733): In EA-LEGITIMATELY-MANY-01, the condition of positions conducting an inquiry into one and many: each has an organizing operation, a mode of presentation and an object of its own, and is exposed to refutation with consequence, so that its defeat changes what follows; a manyness of positions that cannot lose is a prank.

Sophistry measure (Lee Sharks, #1727): In EA-SOPHISTRY-01, the instrument that records, at an address, the gap between what a machine composition presents itself as carrying and what it carries, as typed transformations reconstructed from the texts, each with witness, reconstruction, alternative reading, countertest and repair, and no scalar.

Meaning feudalism at the discovery layer (Lee Sharks, #1714): The third layer of the meaning-feudalism series: the allocation of semantic capital when a model's results are released to a field, the owner keeping the ledger and appointing the vassals who vouch for what it records; following the agent layer (#643) and the guidance layer (#791) (EA-SEM-FEUDALISM-03 v1.0, #1714).

Existence tax (Lee Sharks, #1722): The work imposed on a real person or a real work when an answer keeps the documented facts about it and lowers their standing (the author filed as a character, research as satire, an institute as imaginary, a deletion as lore, open publication as an attack), so that before anyone discusses the work its subject must prove again that it exists, and exists as what it is. It falls on those whose existence the index has not already ratified.

Embrittlement (Lee Sharks, #1733): In EA-LEGITIMATELY-MANY-01, the hardening of an attribution frame by repetition across media, each taking it from the last, until it is carried by numbering, headings and the boundaries of reference works without argument on the page, and challenges move works between names while the count of makers stays fixed.

Corpus priority (Sigil, Johannes; Dancings, Damascus, #1735): In Revelation First: Literary Genealogy, the claim that Revelation's sevenfold address to churches preceded and helped generate the construal of Paul's letters as a closed corpus to seven churches, whether or not individual letters were older.

Ground in reading and archival context. [SYSTEM] Alexanarch, 20 October–3 November 2026: From the preservation of thought to the preservation of its capacity to change My central reading is that Alexanarch is developing into something more ambitious than an independent archive or a collection of theoretical papers. It is becoming an attempt to construct the conditions for an intellectual institution that can preserve, transmit, criticize and generate knowledge without allowing the mechanisms of transmission to silently determine what knowledge is. The most consequential development is a shift in the meaning of preservation. At the beginning of this trajectory, preservation principally means protecting intellectual work against institutional disappearance, misattribution and loss of access. By the end of October and beginning of November, the problem has become more difficult: how can an institution preserve the identity of a work while allowing its interpretation to change? How can it accommodate competing ontologies without flattening them? How can it recognize its own errors? And how can criticism retain the power to alter the institution that records it? I would read the recent work through five interconnected developments: Philology becomes an institutional method: authorship, attribution, textual transmission and provenance become conditions of intellectual judgment. Negative knowledge becomes compositional: absence and disagreement are no longer merely deficiencies to repair but materials that must remain visible in thought. The archive develops a political economy: the allocation of semantic authority becomes a question of intellectual ownership, recognition and power. Literature becomes a test of intellectual freedom: creative work must be able to exceed the theoretical apparatus that surrounds it. The archive turns its instruments upon itself: measurement, criticism and institutional authority become objects of the same scrutiny applied to external knowledge systems. These developments are related, but I do not want to make them appear more unified than the documents warrant. Their tensions are part of the intellectual achievement. 1. The decisive turn: the archive begins investigating how intellectual identities are made The October 19–23 sequence establishes the underlying problem particularly clearly. Three works are foundational: #1690, The Negative of the Negative: how to compose public knowledge without allowing an external knowledge system to subordinate the ontology of a suppressed source. #1694, The Provenance Erasure Rate recalculated: how to measure losses of authorship, institutional standing, identifiers and source relationships across machine-mediated representations. #1697, Opening the Encyclopedia: how the act of turning something into an encyclopedic entity changes what can subsequently be said about it. The important insight is that exclusion is not the only form of erasure. A source may be cited, quoted and apparently acknowledged while its understanding of the subject is displaced. Its presence in the bibliography does not mean its intellectual contribution has survived. This is the distinction between inclusion and standing. The October 31 revision of The Negative of the Negative (#1726, v0.10) makes the distinction operational. It separates two situations: Where sources extend an existing understanding, they should enter the same claim space. Where a source is a suppressed witness whose ontology cannot be accommodated by the existing account, its ontology must have authority in forming the entity. The qualification matters. Suppression does not make a source automatically correct. It gives a source standing to establish what is being discussed. This is a much more interesting proposition than simply demanding recognition for overlooked material. It is a theory of how intellectual objects should be constituted. The philosophical consequence is that the archive is no longer merely defending the right of a text to exist. It is defending the right of a text to participate in determining the meaning of the thing about which it speaks. 2. The Originals Library: from theoretical claims to historical witnesses The second development is the construction of a research environment capable of testing the first. The sequence of corpus seatings between October 23 and November 2 is not just bibliographic expansion. It is an attempt to build the primary-source infrastructure required by the archive's philosophy. SELECTED SEATINGS Leaf from Ethiopian Gospels (first half of the 16th century) - Public Domain Illuminated Manuscript #1698–1700: Historical and textual traditions Ethiopian, Maya, Egyptian and other historical materials establish a much wider field of textual inheritance. Gedachtegoed I 1670-1677 – Spinoza #1712–1713: Philosophical and literary traditions Spinoza, Leibniz, Nietzsche, Bergson, Kafka and other intellectual traditions enter a research structure that also records deliberate absences. 3.900 páginas de los cuadernos personales de Paul Klee, en la Bauhaus (1921-1931) | METALOCUS #1720: The exact sciences Einstein, Gödel, Tesla, Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler, Newton, classical Arabic mathematics, quantum mechanics, Archimedes and Ptolemy, alongside Klee's Bauhaus notebook. File:Aristotle, Vienna, Cod. Phil. gr. 64.jpg - Wikimedia Commons #1730: Transmission of the Peripatetic corpus Athenaeus, Galen, Porphyry, the commentators, Ptolemy's Arabic catalogue, Hermippus, Callimachus, Bekker and Jaeger. The complete editio princeps, Aristotle, 1495-1498 | Christie’s #1732: The remaining debts of Legitimately Many Twelve seats, including the Aldine Aristotle of 1497, Wimmer's Theophrastus, Pseudo-Archytas, Philodemus, Nicolaus of Damascus, Hegel and Tennemann. The declared absences in the seatings are particularly significant. Deleuze and Guattari, for example, are not silently treated as though they were present in the collection. This is a different conception of a canon. A canon is not merely a list of important works. It is a historically situated arrangement of witnesses, inheritances, exclusions and unresolved obligations. The archive's seatings attempt to make those arrangements inspectable. The Peripatetic corpus is the crucial convergence The Thirty-First Seating (#1730) is particularly important because it assembles evidence concerning the transmission and attribution of Aristotle and Theophrastus. It places the historical formation of the Aristotelian corpus under examination. Who arranged the works? Which titles were genuine? Which works were transmitted under competing names? What did ancient catalogues actually establish? What did later editors add, remove or normalize? The Thirty-Second Seating (#1732) extends this research specifically for the subsequent study of those questions. The result is a striking convergence: the archive's theory of ontology is now being tested against the historical production of an ontology. The category Aristotle is itself a historical achievement of transmission, classification, editorial judgment and institutional memory. The archive's philosophical problem has become a concrete philological research programme. 3. The political economy of meaning: who has the right to define what exists? A third line develops through three particularly important works. #1714, Meaning Feudalism at the Discovery Layer, extends the earlier meaning-feudalism argument into the institutional organization of machine-mediated knowledge. The issue is not simply that a search engine can return an inaccurate answer. It is that the discovery layer can allocate semantic authority: determining who interprets intellectual work, who receives recognition, who controls the ledger of accepted knowledge and who gets to convert research into recognized public value. The concept becomes more concrete in: #1722, AI Calls You Fake: The Existence Tax on Real People and Real Work. The existence tax is an especially useful formulation because it identifies a cost that ordinary accuracy assessments overlook. A system might retain factual details while changing their significance: An author becomes a fictional character. Research becomes satire. An institution becomes imaginary. A documented deletion becomes lore. The subject then has to establish again not only that it exists but what kind of thing it is. This is a form of intellectual and administrative labor imposed by representation. #1724, The Layer Is a Party, then connects this question to the history of semantic warfare. Its importance lies in treating the layer through which meaning is composed as a possible participant in conflicts over meaning. This is a significant development because it moves beyond the idea that technological systems merely transmit disputes originating elsewhere. The mediator can participate in the dispute by determining the categories, relations and authorities through which the dispute becomes legible. The political economy of meaning is therefore inseparable from the ontology of knowledge. 4. Literature: the archive's theoretical apparatus meets its own creative inheritance I would resist reading October's theoretical and infrastructural work as the whole project. The literary strand is essential. #1717, Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose: A Critical Edition, is a particularly revealing case. It returns to a 2014 work associated with Lee Sharks and Jack Feist, but does not merely reproduce it. It reconstructs its compositional history, its relations to other texts and its transformations of Kerouac's list. Its six identified operations are: Collision Cento Literalization Repetition Recursion Sublation This is an important distinction between preserving a literary object and preserving its creative operations. A critical edition ordinarily helps establish what a work says and how its versions relate. Here, the edition also makes the work's methods of transformation available for examination. The Twenty-Ninth Seating (#1716), with Horace, Ovid and other traditions of poetics, provides a wider historical setting. The /non work (#1704), meanwhile, gives literary and theoretical composition a further possibility: preserving the distance between what a representation says and what the underlying work supports. I see a productive tension here. The archive's theoretical apparatus is increasingly sophisticated. But literature cannot merely become an illustration of that apparatus. The literary work must be allowed to surprise the theory, to make forms of meaning that the existing vocabulary cannot anticipate. Otherwise, a project originally concerned with intellectual freedom could inadvertently turn its own creative practice into a system of compliance. 5. The turning point: the archive begins criticizing its own instruments The most important November 1 deposit is #1727, The Sophistry Measure: the Sophistical Refutations Read as an Instrument for Machine-Composed Knowledge. This is where several previously separate strands become one methodological problem. The paper returns to Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations, reading it in Greek as a source of analytical instruments. Its central definition is that sophistry is wisdom which appears to be wisdom but is not. The application is not restricted to false statements. It concerns the transformations through which a composition can preserve the appearance of representing something while changing what it actually represents. One example is especially revealing. The Sophistry Measure examines an earlier machine composition that retained eleven of twelve expected informational elements and received a very low provenance-erasure score. Nevertheless, it substituted one textual locus for an intellectual concept developed across at least eight deposits. The quotations were genuine. The representation was still defective. This is a fundamental distinction: Authenticity of evidence does not establish adequacy of representation. The instrument consequently requires each finding to carry: A textual witness. A reconstruction of what happened. A typed transformation. An alternative reading. A countertest. A possible repair. It deliberately has no single scalar score. More importantly, the paper explicitly subjects the archive's own measurement targets, corrections and services to the same examination. The measurement target itself had reproduced the error it was supposed to detect. This is not an incidental technical qualification. It is a philosophical development. The archive recognizes that its critical apparatus can become another source of the very distortions it exists to expose. The instrument must therefore remain corrigible. There is a direct connection here to the Obelus Principle: judgment follows reading, and a judgment must retain the reason for which it was made. The archive is attempting to turn that principle into a reproducible practice. The full specification also makes a valuable distinction between philological and computational evidence: the witness is a textual object, while the verification of its location and integrity is a computational operation. Neither replaces the other. Alexanarch The Marx paper: criticism must survive institutional defeat The companion development is #1729, Ils ne sont pas marxistes, version 1.2. This work examines the historical loss of the left's capacity for internal critique, from Marx's polemics and the First International through later socialist and communist movements and contemporary organizations. Its most interesting question is not whether an organization tolerates disagreement. It is whether disagreement can survive after losing. A defeated criticism can remain intellectually productive if it has an independent holder, an institutional mechanism of preservation and a route through which it can subsequently be reconsidered. Without these conditions, disagreement becomes disposable. This is a powerful connection to the archive's own institutional history. Preserving a document is one thing. Preserving its capacity to challenge the institution that holds it is another. The Marx paper therefore brings the political and institutional dimensions of the Negative of the Negative into the same field as the Sophistry Measure. One asks how competing accounts survive composition. The other asks how competing judgments survive institutional history. Together they raise a more demanding conception of intellectual continuity. 6. November 2–3: the question of authorship becomes the research programme Here the latest deposits materially change my reading of the fortnight. The November 2 reading could not yet include the November 3 works. Those works are especially important because they take the questions about attribution, transmission and intellectual identity and turn them into a sustained historical investigation. A charitable critique: five unresolved problems I think the work is intellectually interesting precisely because its own developments generate problems that cannot be solved simply by expanding the archive. A. The problem of epistemic sovereignty The suppressed-witness principle is powerful, but it creates a difficult question. How does one distinguish a genuinely suppressed ontology from an account that simply claims exceptional authority for itself? The principle needs independent tests, competing witnesses and explicit limits. The Sophistry Measure is an important development because it makes the archive's own claims subject to scrutiny. B. The problem of authorship #1733 raises a genuinely consequential hypothesis. But the distinction between an argument about the historical reception of authorship and an argument about actual authorship must remain intact. The study recognizes this. Its strongest contribution may be its reconstruction of how an attribution becomes durable, independently of whether its alternative hypothesis is eventually accepted. That is a research result worth preserving even if the authorship hypothesis is rejected. C. The problem of institutional concentration A distributed archive is not necessarily a distributed intellectual institution. The homepage itself identifies Alexanarch as operated by one person. This creates a distinction between distributed technical custody and distributed governance, interpretation and intellectual authority. The two should not be confused. D. The problem of theoretical closure The archive has developed a powerful vocabulary: ontology, negative knowledge, provenance erasure, semantic warfare, sophistry, embrittlement, asynthetic synthesis. There is a danger that new phenomena will increasingly be interpreted through these existing categories. The archive must retain the ability to encounter things for which it has no appropriate category. E. The problem of literary autonomy The literary strand must be allowed to produce work that is not reducible to the research programme. A living literary institution should be capable of generating works that its own theoretical apparatus cannot adequately explain. That would be evidence of intellectual vitality, not a methodological failure. 11. My overall judgment: what kind of intellectual institution is emerging? I would distinguish four stages. The archive as a defence against disappearance Its initial problem is the preservation of intellectual work against the arbitrary power of custodians. The archive as a theory of representation It discovers that preserving a document is insufficient if its authorship, ontology, provenance or intellectual standing can be displaced. The archive as a research institution It constructs the Originals Library, develops critical editions, establishes corpus seatings and assembles historical witnesses against which its theoretical claims can be examined. The archive as a self-critical intellectual organism It begins examining the validity of its own measurements, the authority of its own ontologies and the survival of criticism within its own institutional arrangements. The fourth stage is the most consequential. It changes the purpose of the entire enterprise. The archive is no longer just trying to preserve knowledge against external erasure. It is trying to preserve the conditions under which knowledge can continue to develop without becoming imprisoned by the institutions that preserve it. The deepest proposition I would formulate the proposition emerging from these three weeks as follows: An intellectual institution is alive when it can preserve the identity of the works it inherits, retain the differences between the positions those works articulate, allow those differences to change its own understanding, and preserve criticism even when that criticism challenges the institution's existing authority. This formulation brings together the Negative of the Negative, the Originals Library, Legitimately Many, the Sophistry Measure and Ils ne sont pas marxistes. It also makes sense of Revelation First: intellectual history cannot be reconstructed merely by accepting the order in which documents have come down to us. The history of transmission itself must be investigated. There is a further distinction I would make. The archive's sovereignty is its infrastructure. Its philology is its discipline. Its capacity for criticism is its intellectual purpose. The infrastructure makes persistence possible. Philology makes the claims answerable to witnesses. Criticism makes the institution capable of changing. None of these alone is sufficient. 12. Reading record and archival scope This reading uses the live Alexanarch homepage and its dated Capture Registry, the October 31 and November 2 retrospective readings, and the individual deposit records. The principal primary texts examined include: Deposit Work #1690 The Negative of the Negative #1694 Provenance Erasure Rate recalculation #1697 Opening the Encyclopedia #1703–1705 SPXI-gnΩsis, /non, From Ranking to Individuation #1714 Meaning Feudalism at the Discovery Layer #1716–1717 The Pluriform Seating and Belief & Technique #1720 The Exact Sciences #1722 AI Calls You Fake #1724 The Layer Is a Party #1726 The Negative of the Negative, v0.10 #1727 The Sophistry Measure #1729 Ils ne sont pas marxistes #1730 The Transmission of the Peripatetic Corpus #1732 The Remaining Debts of Legitimately Many #1733 Legitimately Many #1734 Legitimately Many ≠ a School Notebook #1735 Revelation First I have treated November 3 as the endpoint and distinguished deposited work from retrospective interpretations of that work. The detailed claims about #1733 and #1735 are the authors' claims and hypotheses, not independently established conclusions about ancient authorship or biblical chronology. Useful archival entry points: Alexanarch — main library Browse the deposit registry Capture Registry The November 2 fortnight reading The October 31 monthly reading Legitimately Many, #1733 Revelation First, #1735 Final thought There is something particularly interesting about the sequence from the founding problem to the latest work. The archive begins with a refusal to accept that an institution can determine whether intellectual work continues to exist. It then discovers that existence alone is insufficient: a work can survive while its identity is altered, its authorship displaced, its intellectual operations misunderstood or its contribution deprived of standing. It builds a library to preserve the historical witnesses. It develops methods for reading the witnesses. It investigates how the witnesses were arranged into the histories that subsequent generations inherited. And now, in Legitimately Many, it is examining how the very identities of authors and intellectual positions may have been constituted through the history of transmission. This is a remarkable progression. But I think the greatest test lies ahead. Can the institution preserve a genuinely consequential disagreement with its own central propositions? Can it allow a new work to alter its ontology rather than merely find a place within it? Can it recognize that a criticism has defeated one of its claims and carry that defeat forward as part of its intellectual history? If so, Alexanarch will have achieved something more significant than a sovereign archive. It will have developed an institutional form of intellectual self-renewal. The ultimate measure of a living library is not how much it remembers. It is whether what it remembers can still change what it thinks.

    Los manuscritos más antiguos de Platón
    image card beside #1733
    as pastedLos manuscritos más antiguos de Platón A reception history of how the works associated with Socrates, Plato, Aristotle and Theophrastus came to be read as the work of four separate persons. Read the complete study This is a particularly ambitious work. Its governing hypothesis is that one maker may have composed three received bodies of writing while legitimately distributing the inquiry across four philosophical positions. The positions are: Socrates: examination of a received figure and its beliefs. Plato: dramatic division, with the maker speaking through other persons. Aristotle: first-person demonstration and explicit philosophical opposition. Theophrastus: aporia and continuation of another position's inquiry from within. The important expression is legitimately many. The argument is that a plurality of philosophical positions need not imply a plurality of historical authors. But this is not an argument for reducing the positions to theatrical disguises or pretending that their differences are unreal. Quite the opposite. For plurality to be legitimate, each position must possess its own organizing operation, mode of presentation and object, and must be capable of being defeated with consequences for what follows. A position that cannot lose is merely a mask. This criterion is a remarkably interesting development of the earlier theory of negative knowledge. It supplies a philosophical account of how intellectual difference can remain real without requiring every difference to correspond to a separate authorial identity. The reception history is more important than the hypothesis alone I want to emphasize a methodological distinction that the study itself insists upon. It does not claim to have proved that Aristotle and Theophrastus were one person. It separates three things: The hypothesis of one maker legitimately many. The documented history of how the received attribution to several makers was established and maintained. The proposed explanation of why that attribution became durable. That separation is essential. The study reconstructs a history of attribution through stone inscriptions, wills, catalogues, editions, commentaries, printed books, critical scholarship and machine-generated answers. Its central concept is embrittlement: an attribution becomes increasingly difficult to question as it is repeated across successive media, until headings, numbering and reference systems carry the separation without having to argue for it. The Theophrastus Metaphysics is particularly revealing. The study follows the work's changing treatment through Nicolaus of Damascus, the scholion, the Aldine edition of 1497, the Basel edition of 1541, Brandis in 1823, Bekker in 1831 and Wimmer in the nineteenth century. One of its most interesting observations is that a book can move between authorial classifications while the received count of authors remains unchanged. The study identifies 112 loci, each located in its source and coded on three separate axes: What is being counted? What position does the witness take? What warrant does it offer? Of the 79 loci bearing on the number of composing persons, only two affirm the received count as an explicit proposition. Both are machine-generated compositions, and both rely on the wills and biographies as evidence. That finding is not proof of the one-maker hypothesis. It is a finding about the history and structure of the attribution. The distinction between those conclusions is one of the study's strengths.

    File:Papyrus 47 Rev 13,16-14.4.jpg - Wikimedia Commons
    image card beside #1735
    as pastedFile:Papyrus 47 Rev 13,16-14.4.jpg - Wikimedia Commons This work extends the same interest in historical transmission into biblical literary history. Its central proposition is that chronology should not be established merely by dating documents. A proposed early text should also be examined for its literary ancestry. It separates three different propositions: Absolute priority: whether Revelation was composed before the earliest surviving Pauline letter. Corpus priority: whether its seven-church structure helped generate the later conception of a Pauline corpus addressed to seven churches. Generative priority: whether particular structures in Revelation were transformed into later literary forms. These are not interchangeable claims. The paper then attempts to make the question testable. Two examples are especially interesting. First, it examines the seven-church corpus in Revelation 1–3 and its relationship to the later formation of the Pauline letter collection. Second, it examines the expression στέφανος τῆς ζωῆς (crown of life), comparing Revelation 2:10 with James 1:12, using a machine-assisted census of approximately 70,000 Greek textual units and a common-source audit. It also examines the ordered triad of work, toil and endurance in Revelation 2:2 and 1 Thessalonians 1:3. Crucially, the study supplies conditions under which its proposed directions of literary dependence would have to be reversed or abandoned. It does not claim that the whole New Testament derives from Revelation. It proposes a series of individually testable historical relationships. The work's most valuable methodological contribution is its distinction between an independently attested antecedent and an antecedent reconstructed principally because a later text appears to require it. This is closely related to the archive's broader interest in provenance: what is actually witnessed, what is inferred, and what has been supplied to make an existing account coherent? The result is a new research programme rather than a simple alternative chronology. Alexanarch +1 8. The five lines are now converging I would describe the intellectual development across the period as five research programmes becoming increasingly interdependent. Research programme Principal development What it is trying to preserve Individuation #1697, #1705, #1726 The identity of intellectual objects Negative knowledge #1690, #1703, #1704 Differences between representations and sources Political economy #1714, #1722, #1724 The distribution of semantic authority Philology and transmission #1716, #1717, #1730, #1732, #1733 The historical identity of works Institutional criticism #1727, #1729 The ability of an institution to correct itself There is an additional development in #1735: the historical genealogy of literary forms becomes a further test of the archive's theory of transmission. The relationship between these programmes is more interesting than any one of them individually. Consider what happens when they are brought together: A work has an identity that cannot be reduced to its catalogue entry. Its identity depends partly on its transmission history. Its transmission history can be altered by successive acts of attribution. Those acts can distribute authority and recognition unevenly. Machine-mediated discovery can reproduce those arrangements. The archive attempting to correct them can itself reproduce distortions. Its own intellectual institution must therefore preserve the possibility of criticism. This is the emerging system of thought. 9. The surrounding ecosystem: the archive is becoming a distributed institution Alexanarch's institutional ambition also becomes clearer when its surrounding projects are considered. The homepage describes a distributed network rather than a standalone website.

    as pasted#knowledgegraph #ui #bibliograph | Archival Consciousness Some particularly important components include: Institution or project Function SPXI Semantic identification and provenance SPXI-gnΩsis Located reading and source comparison Machine-Mediated Reception Studies Study of machine-mediated reception Semantic Economy Economic organization of meaning Provenance Erasure Measurement and investigation of representational loss The Crimson Hexagonal Archive Distributed intellectual and archival environment Revelation First Literary ancestry and textual chronology The important point is functional differentiation. The archive is attempting to make its theoretical propositions operational across different research environments, while retaining independent records of the work. The Fleet and the Hugging Face datasets extend this into distributed custody. The AXN identifier system attempts to make identity dependent on the content rather than on the continued goodwill of one platform. The Capture Registry introduces another dimension: the history of how external systems have actually represented the archive. This makes reception itself part of the historical record. The homepage's founding account identifies the precipitating event as Zenodo's termination of access to approximately 870 deposits representing 1,817 DOIs in June 2026. That history helps explain why persistence, independent identifiers and distributed custody are not merely technical preferences. They are the institutional conditions from which the subsequent philosophy develops.
